## Welcome back — the capstone session

The last three sessions each introduced new techniques, one at a time, and asked you to apply them to the same running shape-categorization experiment. Today is different: **no new techniques**. Instead, you'll choose a classic cognitive psychology task, and build it yourself — from a specification, not step-by-step instructions — using only what you already know.

This mirrors real research practice: nobody hands you a tutorial for the specific experiment you want to run. You start from a task description and a blank file, and assemble it from techniques you already have.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this session you will be able to:

- Independently assemble a complete jsPsych experiment from a specification, without step-by-step instructions.
- Choose and implement a classic cognitive psychology task (Stroop, Flanker, lexical decision, or a scaffolded visual search).
- Host a finished experiment on GitHub Pages and send its data to the Open Science Framework, so it could genuinely be run by remote participants.
:::

---

### Getting set up

```
session4-template/
├── experiment.html    <- minimal starter shell: plugins linked, empty timeline
├── cheatsheet.md       <- quick syntax reference for everything above
├── consent/            <- optional fuller consent form, from Session 3
└── jspsych/            <- jsPsych core + every plugin you might need
```

`experiment.html` is deliberately close to empty — just the plugin `<script>` tags and `const timeline = [];`. No task-specific code is provided; that's the point of today. Keep `cheatsheet.md` open in a second window while you work.

## The Specification

Whichever task you choose, your finished experiment must include all of the following — this is what "done" means today, regardless of which task you picked:

::: {.callout-important}
## Required components
1. A **consent screen** (simple Y/N, or the fuller external file — your choice).
2. A **participant ID** trial, tagged onto all data with `addProperties()`.
3. An **instructions screen** explaining the task and response keys.
4. A **fixation cross** before every single stimulus trial, in both practice and main blocks (Session 2, Part 1.3) — without it, one stimulus just replaces another with no warning, which makes it hard to tell whether the display changed or a response was even registered.
5. A **practice block** with feedback after every trial.
6. A **main block**, with **no feedback**, using **timeline variables** (not a hand-written loop) for at least one randomized factor.
7. **RT and accuracy** recorded for every main-block trial.
8. A **debrief screen** reporting the participant's own accuracy and mean RT.
9. Data **saved** to a file, with the participant ID and a timestamp in the filename.
:::

Everything in this list has a corresponding entry in the recap table above — if you get stuck on *how*, that's where to look.

---

## Choosing a Task

Pick one. All four are matched in overall structure — instructions, practice, main block, one randomized factor — so the specification above applies identically regardless of which you choose.

::: {.callout-important}
## A new wrinkle: combining two timeline variables

For Stroop, each trial needs **both** the word (e.g. "RED") **and** the ink color (e.g. "blue") to build one piece of HTML: `"<p style='color:blue;'>RED</p>"`. Every timeline-variable trial you built in Session 3 only ever plugged in *one* value directly:

```js
stimulus: jsPsych.timelineVariable("image")
```

This works because `jsPsych.timelineVariable("image")` doesn't actually hand you the image path when this line runs. It returns a special marker that jsPsych recognizes — think of it like a Post-it note that says "put the real `image` value here once you know which stimulus is current." jsPsych goes looking for these Post-it notes right before showing each trial, and swaps in the real value at that point.

**The problem: you can't glue two Post-it notes together with `+` and get a real sentence.** If you tried:

```js
// This does NOT work:
stimulus: "<p style='color:" + jsPsych.timelineVariable("color") + "'>" + jsPsych.timelineVariable("word") + "</p>"
```

...the `+` runs immediately, the moment your script builds this trial object — long before jsPsych knows which stimulus is "current." All you have at that moment is two Post-it notes, and gluing text onto a Post-it note just gives you the note's generic label. That's why you'll see the literal text `[object Object]` show up on screen instead of your word.

**The fix: write a function**, exactly like Session 2, Part 3's feedback trial (`stimulus: function() {...}`). jsPsych calls this function fresh, right before every single trial — at the exact moment it *does* know the current stimulus. But there's one more twist: **inside your own function, `jsPsych.timelineVariable("word")` still only gives you the inert Post-it note**, not the real word — jsPsych only swaps in real values for Post-it notes sitting directly in specific trial settings, not ones buried inside code you wrote yourself. Instead, use **`jsPsych.evaluateTimelineVariable("word")`** inside the function — the "give me the real value, right now" version, built specifically for this situation:

```js
stimulus: function () {
  let word = jsPsych.evaluateTimelineVariable("word");
  let color = jsPsych.evaluateTimelineVariable("color");
  return "<p style='color:" + color + ";'>" + word + "</p>";
}
```

**The rule of thumb:**

- Plugging in exactly *one* value, directly as a trial parameter? Use `jsPsych.timelineVariable("name")` — same as Session 3, nothing new.
- Combining values, or building a piece of text yourself inside a function? Use `jsPsych.evaluateTimelineVariable("name")` inside that function instead.

You'll hit this with Stroop (word + color), Flanker (two arrow directions), and visual search (target presence + position) — anywhere a single stimulus needs to be built from more than one piece of information.
:::

### Stroop task

Participants see a color word (e.g. "RED") printed in an ink color that may or may not match the word, and respond to the **ink color**, ignoring the word.

- **Randomized factor**: congruency (word matches ink color, or doesn't) — built from the full combination of words × colors.
- **Stimulus**: plain HTML/CSS, e.g. `"<p style='color:blue;'>RED</p>"`.
- **Response**: one key per color (e.g. R / G / B / Y).

### Flanker task

Participants see a central arrow flanked by other arrows, and respond to the **direction of the central arrow only**.

- **Randomized factor**: congruency (flankers point the same way as the center, or the opposite way).
- **Stimulus**: plain text arrows, e.g. `"<p style='font-size:48px;'><<<<<</p>"` (congruent, pointing left) vs. `"<p style='font-size:48px;'><<><<</p>"` (incongruent — center points right).
- **Response**: one key per direction (e.g. F for left, J for right).

### Lexical decision task

Participants see a string of letters and decide whether it's a real word or not.

- **Randomized factor**: lexicality (real word vs. made-up nonword).
- **Stimulus**: plain text, e.g. `"<p style='font-size:36px;'>TABLE</p>"` vs. `"<p style='font-size:36px;'>FLOOP</p>"`. You'll need to write your own small word list and nonword list (8–12 of each is plenty).
- **Response**: one key for "real word," one for "not a real word."

### Visual search *(scaffolded)*

Participants search for a target letter ("T") among distractor letters ("L"s), scattered around the screen, and indicate whether the target is present or absent.

Unlike the other three tasks, positioning several letters on screen needs a bit of scaffolding — CSS positioning wasn't covered in Sessions 1–3 in this much detail. Here's a fixed set of 6 screen positions you can use directly:

```js
const positions = [
  { top: "20%", left: "20%" }, { top: "20%", left: "50%" }, { top: "20%", left: "80%" },
  { top: "70%", left: "20%" }, { top: "70%", left: "50%" }, { top: "70%", left: "80%" }
];
```

Each letter is an absolutely-positioned `<span>` inside your `stimulus` HTML, e.g.:

```js
"<div style='position:relative; height:300px;'>" +
  "<span style='position:absolute; top:20%; left:50%;'>T</span>" +
  "<span style='position:absolute; top:70%; left:20%;'>L</span>" +
  // ... one span per letter, using the positions array above
"</div>"
```

- **Randomized factor**: whether the target is present (and if so, at which of the 6 positions) or absent altogether.
- **Response**: one key for "target present," one for "target absent."

### N-back *(optional stretch goal only)*

Participants see a sequence of items and respond whenever the current item matches the one shown **n** positions earlier. This genuinely goes beyond Sessions 1–3: it requires comparing the current trial against one several trials in the past, which `timeline_variables` doesn't give you directly.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint, if you want to attempt N-back anyway
`jsPsych.data.get()` returns *all* data collected so far — including trials from several steps back, not just the last one (`Session 3` only used `.last(1)`). You'd need `.last(n)` or manual indexing into the returned array to compare the current trial's stimulus to the one shown `n` trials earlier, inside `on_finish`. This is meaningfully harder than anything else today — attempt it only once your chosen main task is fully working.
:::

---

## Independent Build Time

Work through the specification for your chosen task. A few suggestions:

::: {.callout-tip}
## Suggested order
1. Get a single stimulus trial working first (no practice/main split, no consent, no saving) — just confirm the core response logic works and scores correctly.
2. Add your `stimulus_list` and convert to `timeline_variables`.
3. Add practice (with feedback) and main (without) blocks.
4. Add consent, participant ID, and data saving.
5. Add the debrief screen last — it depends on everything before it already working and tagging `phase`/`correct` correctly.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## If you get stuck
Check `cheatsheet.md` for the relevant syntax pattern first. If the *logic* (not just syntax) isn't clicking, flag down the instructor — today is about applying what you know, not guessing at material that hasn't been covered.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Worked solutions
A complete worked solution for every task on the menu (Stroop, Flanker, lexical decision, visual search, and even the N-back stretch goal) will be posted on the [Templates & Materials](../materials.qmd) page the day after the session — a good way to compare approaches once you've built your own.
:::

## Going Live

A finished experiment sitting on your own laptop isn't yet something a participant elsewhere could run. Two pieces make that possible.

### Hosting: GitHub Pages

You should already have a GitHub account from the Session 3 homework. Here's the full process, step by step.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Step-by-step: from project folder to live URL

1. **Rename your main file to `index.html`.** GitHub Pages automatically serves a file called `index.html` at your site's root URL. If your file is still called `experiment.html`, rename it now — this saves you from having to type an extra `/experiment.html` on the end of every link you share.

2. **Create a new repository.**
   - Go to <https://github.com/new>.
   - Give it a name (e.g. `stroop-experiment`) — no spaces, lowercase is safest.
   - Set it to **Public** (GitHub Pages on a free account requires a public repository).
   - Leave "Add a README file" unchecked — you don't need one.
   - Click **Create repository**.

3. **Upload your project files.**
   - On your new repository's page, click **"Add file" → "Upload files."**
   - Drag your *entire* project folder's contents into the browser window — `index.html`, the `jspsych/` folder, `consent/` if you're using it, and any other files/folders. Modern GitHub supports dragging whole folders in at once; the folder structure is preserved.
   - Scroll down and click **"Commit changes."**
   - Double check afterwards that `jspsych/jspsych.js` and the other plugin files actually appear *inside* a `jspsych` folder in your repository, not loose at the top level — a common mistake is only dragging the files inside a folder without the folder itself, which breaks every `<script src="jspsych/...">` path.

4. **Enable GitHub Pages.**
   - Go to your repository's **Settings** tab, then **Pages** in the left sidebar.
   - Under "Build and deployment" → "Source," select **"Deploy from a branch."**
   - Under "Branch," select **`main`** and folder **`/ (root)`**, then click **Save**.
   - Wait 1–2 minutes. Refresh the Pages settings page — a message will appear: *"Your site is live at https://your-username.github.io/your-repo-name/"*.

5. **Test the link yourself first**, in a private/incognito browser window (so you're not accidentally logged into anything that might affect the experiment), before sharing it with anyone else.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Debugging corner
If your live page shows a blank screen or a 404, the most common causes are: the repository is private (must be Public), you selected the wrong branch/folder when enabling Pages, or your file isn't actually named `index.html`. If images or the jsPsych library don't load, check that folder names in your `<script src="...">` and `<img src="...">` tags exactly match the folder names as uploaded — capitalization matters on GitHub Pages even if it didn't seem to on your own computer.
:::

### Saving data: two options

You should already have GitHub, OSF, and DataPipe accounts from the homework set at the end of Session 3 — today is about using them, not creating them.

::: {.callout-note}
## Option A: DataPipe → OSF (recommended default)
**DataPipe** is a free service, built by the jsPsych team, that sends your experiment's data straight to an Open Science Framework (OSF) project, with no backend server required — which is exactly what makes it work on free static hosting like GitHub Pages.

```html
<script src="https://unpkg.com/@jspsych-contrib/plugin-pipe"></script>
```

```js
const save_data_trial = {
  type: jsPsychPipe,
  action: "save",
  experiment_id: "YOUR_DATAPIPE_EXPERIMENT_ID",
  filename: participant_id_value + "_" + build_timestamp() + ".csv",
  data_string: () => jsPsych.data.get().csv()
};
```

Add `save_data_trial` as the very last item in your timeline.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Step-by-step: finding your experiment ID and testing it actually works

1. **Find your DataPipe experiment ID.** Log in at <https://pipe.jspsych.org>, open the experiment you created as Session 3 homework, and copy its experiment ID — it's shown on the experiment's own page on the DataPipe dashboard.
2. **Paste it into your code**, replacing `"YOUR_DATAPIPE_EXPERIMENT_ID"` above, exactly as shown (keep the quotes).
3. **Important: this will *not* work by double-clicking your `index.html` file locally.** DataPipe needs your experiment to be loaded over `http://` or `https://` (i.e. actually hosted, via GitHub Pages or Live Server) — opening a file directly from your computer's file system (a `file://` address) will fail silently or show a network error in the console, since browsers block this kind of request from local files.
4. **Run your experiment via your live GitHub Pages link** (not locally) all the way to the end.
5. **Check your OSF project.** Open the OSF project you linked to this DataPipe experiment, and look inside its data component (created automatically when you set up DataPipe). A new file should appear almost immediately, named whatever you set `filename` to.
6. If nothing appears: double check that **both "data collection" and "base64 data collection" are enabled**, and **"data validation" is disabled**, in your DataPipe experiment's settings (these are the settings from the Session 3 homework) — a mismatch here is the most common reason data silently fails to arrive.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Option B: `.localSave()` + participants email you the file
If you're recruiting through **ERAS** and sharing a GitHub Pages link that way, a simpler option is to keep `.localSave()` exactly as you've been using it — the participant's browser downloads their own data as a CSV file at the end — and ask participants to **email you that file** afterwards.

This works, but it only works fairly and smoothly if participants know about it *before* they start:

- **Say so explicitly in your information letter or initial correspondence**, before participants begin: that completing the experiment will download a data file to their own computer, and that they're asked to email it to you (give the exact email address) in order to receive their course credit / compensation. Don't leave this as a surprise at the end.
- Ask them to **keep the participant ID they entered** consistent with whatever identifier ERAS uses to track credit, so you can match an incoming email to the right person.
- **Credit participants once you've received their file** — check the email against your ERAS participant list, and grant credit only for files actually received, the same way you'd track completion for any in-person study.

This is a reasonable, real-world fallback — plenty of published studies have used exactly this pattern — but Option A (DataPipe) is more robust: data arrives immediately and automatically, with no dependence on the participant remembering to send an email.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## A simpler alternative: cognition.run
[cognition.run](https://www.cognition.run) is a more fully managed hosting platform built specifically for jsPsych experiments — it handles both hosting and data storage together, at the cost of being less flexible than GitHub Pages + DataPipe. Worth knowing about if you want something more turnkey for your own future projects.
:::

## Wrap-up: Run Each Other's Experiments

Once your experiment is live, share your GitHub Pages link with a classmate and actually run their experiment as a real participant — press keys, make mistakes, read your own debrief screen. This is both a satisfying end to four sessions of building, and a genuine test that hosting and data saving actually worked, from someone else's computer rather than your own.

---

## Summary

Over four sessions, you went from "what is an `<h1>` tag" to a complete, independently-built, publicly-hosted experiment with real data collection. Specifically, today you:

- Assembled a full experiment from a specification, choosing your own task.
- Combined every technique from Sessions 1–3 — trials, timelines, timeline variables, consent, data saving, debriefing — without step-by-step guidance.
- Took an experiment from your own laptop to a real, publicly accessible URL, with data flowing to a real OSF project.

Whatever you build today is yours to keep, adapt, and extend — for a real pilot study, a class project, or simply as a working example the next time you need to build something similar in jsPsych.
